assessment: Full assembly plausibly provides a physical completeness check and a starting arrangement, while retaining rearrangeability; these benefits are hypotheses. Recorded absence of damage supports retaining current packaging provisionally. Performance remains short of the time target, with only seven of ten observed customers succeeding unaided. Five component complaints suggest a contents problem but do not establish five verified packing errors. The concrete limiting observation is that both workers finish repeated three-compartment orders in seven to nine minutes: assembly is not uniformly slow. All six extreme delays occurred in mixed batches, but layout complexity and switching remain confounded. Overlapping partition widths likewise do not identify the cause of insertion retries.

openings.claim: Order switching during selection and checking may explain part of the mixed-batch delay and contents errors; staging one complete order together before insertion may help.
openings.delta: Localizes a potentially avoidable cost within the incumbent assembled workflow.
openings.prediction: For comparable layouts, staging reduces selection/checking time and discrepancies while insertion time remains similar. If insertion dominates instead, this account weakens.
openings.probe: Use existing spare-board samples for paired builds under current selection versus one-order staging, alternating sequence and balancing workers and layout counts. Log selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, plus required-part discrepancies. Reuse a bench area; keep dimensions, parts, colors and packaging unchanged.
assumptions: Bench staging fits the available space without blocking the other worker.
Sample work fits existing delivery slack; do not delay accepted orders.

openings.claim: The generic three-layout diagram may leave the short partition's ordered position ambiguous even when all correct parts are supplied.
openings.delta: Separates instruction ambiguity from missing parts and insertion difficulty.
openings.prediction: An order-specific diagram reduces short-partition questions and unaided arrangement failures despite identical, verified contents.
openings.probe: Randomly assign ten willing participants to current or order-specific diagrams using verified sample organizers. Record first-exposure arrangement success, short-partition questions and insertion failures. Treat this small comparison as directional evidence.
assumptions: Diagram preparation and reproduction stay within the initial 500 and recurring 0.40 limits and the fixed delivery date.
Ordered counts, colors, capacity, footprint and detachable construction are retained.
